overview: The Aché are Indigenous communities of eastern Paraguay whose histories include forest hunting and gathering, violent dispossession, settlement and continuing cultural work. Research on Northern Aché families documents practical knowledge, cooperation and changing livelihoods; it should not be treated as a description of every Aché community.

periods.title: Capture, violence and displacement
periods.summary: Captures and massacres in the twentieth century forcibly disrupted Aché life. Paraguay’s census history records attacks from 1959 to 1972 and international denunciations of genocide and ethnocide in 1974.

periods.title: Settlement and continued forest work
periods.summary: Chupa Pou was established in 1978. Northern Aché residents combined farming with forest trips; early 1980s fieldwork records changes in labour and household life.

periods.title: Restitution and cultural work
periods.summary: Returns of ancestral remains in 2010 and 2012 and later community language projects document continuing Aché efforts to shape how their heritage is treated.

items.text: A child’s bow from Arroyo Bandera, now in the Museo de América, was made before 1997. Its slightly curved wooden body carries a twisted plant-fibre string secured around both ends. The object preserves the combination of carving, cord-making and binding needed to produce working equipment.

The museum names the bow rapa and records separate Aché terms for its wood and cord fibre. Its account also describes using an unstrung bow to reach animals in burrows. Such versatility connects tool design with detailed knowledge of different hunting situations.

An Aché arrow at the Spencer Museum combines bamboo, wood, plant fibre, resin and feathers tentatively identified as guan. Its maker is unrecorded, and its date spans the late nineteenth century to 1976. The catalogue supports a study of material selection, not an exact manufacturing year or excavated findspot.

At Chupa Pou in 1981 to 1982, researchers observed maize, manioc, beans, peanuts and other crops. Groups cleared and planted large fields, while some men began smaller plots. Farming arrangements were changing within the settlement itself, rather than representing a timeless Aché agricultural system.

The same fieldwork describes men and women moving a temporary brush barricade through a lagoon to concentrate fish. Springs supplied domestic water, while rivers and streams served washing and bathing. These observations connect collective fishing skill with the practical organisation of settlement life.

Forest foods in the Northern Aché studies included hunted mammals, honey, palm starch, fruit and larvae. Obtaining a meal required several kinds of work and knowledge. Researchers describe different contributions by men and women, with patterns tied to the studied trips and households rather than universal rules.

Food gathered on forest trips was distributed widely between families, particularly meat and honey. The authors compared those trips with life at Arroyo Bandera in 1998, where food was more often directed toward families who shared similar foods back. Cooperation changed with residence and production.

Settlement livelihoods also included paid work and occasional sales of palm-woven fans, mats, bows and arrows. Purchased foods and tools entered household economies alongside farming and forest resources. Cultural continuity could include participating in new markets, rather than preserving one fixed way of obtaining everything.

sections.title: Historical records and the return of ancestors

items.text: Paraguay’s Indigenous-community census history describes captures and a massacre between 1959 and 1972, followed by international denunciations in 1974. The violent breakup of forest communities cannot be described simply as voluntary modernisation. The record identifies assaults on people, not the end of Aché existence.

Archival research reconstructed the fate of an Aché girl called Damiana, abducted in 1897 and taken to Argentina. After her death, remains entered scientific collections associated with racial investigation. Letters and publications helped identify material later located in Berlin, exposing violence within the history of collecting.

La Plata returned remains to the Aché community in 2010; Berlin returned further identified remains in 2012. The researchers explicitly recognised the community’s wish for burial. These events changed the relationship between institutions and the people whose ancestors they had held.

In August 2025, teachers and representatives from six Aché communities met at Cerro Morotĩ to review and correct a dictionary draft. Community members and LETRA Paraguay had developed the material together. This was active editorial and linguistic work, not merely outsiders recording passive informants.

The national language secretariat’s digital vocabulary page credits members of the Aché people as authors and LETRA Paraguay as compiler. Online and mobile resources extend language work into new media. Their availability documents a continuing language project without establishing how widely each resource is used.

ending.text: Aché communities survived campaigns of capture and violence and continue to maintain language and collective institutions. Dispossession transformed residence and livelihoods, but it did not produce a historical extinction date. The imported map ends at 1500 because its snapshot interval ends there, not because Aché history stopped.
